explanations.answer: The house of Israel and the royal house
explanations.explanation: You listened, baker. The LORD says, “Hear this, O priests! Take heed, O house of Israel! Give ear, O royal house!” That's three groups called by name. Nobody gets to say it was meant for the person standing next to them.

explanations.answer: The prophets and the elders of the land
explanations.explanation: Prophets and elders sound official, but they aren't on this list. The LORD names the priests, the house of Israel and the royal house. When a message has names on it, you check the names. These three are the ones He calls.

explanations.answer: The soldiers and the judges at the gate
explanations.explanation: Soldiers and judges would make a mighty serious meeting, but the LORD doesn't call them here. He says, “Take heed, O house of Israel! Give ear, O royal house!” So the other two are the people of Israel and the king's household. Priests, Israel and the royal house is the whole guest list.

Right on the money. The LORD says they have been “…a snare at Mizpah, a net spread out on Tabor.” Mizpah and Tabor are the two places He names. A snare and a net are both made to catch someone, and nobody spreads one out as a welcome mat.

A pit is a trapping picture too, so I see why it tempted you. But the text says “…a net spread out on Tabor.” The LORD picks a net, so we keep the net. I'd have to dig a whole new verse to fit a pit in there.

No fire here, friend. The LORD says they have been “…a snare at Mizpah, a net spread out on Tabor.” I know fire. I've watched a tray of cookies go from golden to charcoal while I looked the other way. But this verse talks about a snare and a net.
Close, but the verse goes bigger than that. The LORD says, “but I will chastise them all.” He doesn't say only the worst of them. One little word, all, and it covers everybody.

That's it. The LORD says the rebels are deep in slaughter, “but I will chastise them all.” Not just the worst of them, all of them. This is a heavy verse, and I think it's meant to be taken seriously.
Yes, defiled. The LORD says, “I know all about Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from Me.” Then He says, “Israel is defiled.” He isn't guessing here. He knows all about it.
Blameless would be a nice word, but it's the opposite of what the LORD says. In this verse He says, “Israel is defiled.” He also says Israel is not hidden from Him. So there's no hiding a thing.

Nothing about money in this verse, friend. The LORD says He knows all about Ephraim and then says, “Israel is defiled.” That's the word that fits the blank. Prosperous belongs in some other verse, not this one.

I understand the guess, but the text says the opposite. The LORD says a spirit of prostitution is within them, “…and they do not know the LORD.” So they don't know Him. That sentence is short and it doesn't leave room to wiggle.

Correct. Hosea 5:4 says a spirit of prostitution is within them, “…and they do not know the LORD.” It also says their deeds do not permit them to return to their God. So this is about people who don't know Him, not people who still do.

Judah would be the one still standing steady in this crowd, but the verse says otherwise. It says, “Israel and Ephraim stumble in their iniquity; even Judah stumbles with them.” The word “even” is the giveaway. Judah stumbles right along with the rest.
You got it. The verse says, “even Judah stumbles with them.” Judah followed the house of David (1 Kings 12:20), and it still stumbles here. When you see the word “even,” brace yourself.
That's right, baker. They go with their flocks and herds to seek the LORD, “…but they do not find Him…” The verse adds that “He has withdrawn Himself from them.” That stings.

The verse doesn't say a word about priests turning anybody away. It says they go with flocks and herds to seek the LORD, “…but they do not find Him…” So the people show up and the LORD isn't found. I won't add a door and a doorman that the text never put there.

No thieves are named in this verse, friend. The people go with their flocks and herds to seek the LORD, “…but they do not find Him…” That's what happens here, and the verse says He has withdrawn Himself from them. So the answer is that they don't find Him.

explanations.answer: He has withdrawn Himself from them
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. They seek Him and don't find Him, because “He has withdrawn Himself from them.” This is a sobering verse. The LORD doesn't leave it as a mystery, either. He tells us right there that He withdrew.

explanations.answer: He has sent them to the prophets
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say He sent them anywhere. It says, “He has withdrawn Himself from them.” That's the reason they don't find Him. I'll keep it exactly as the verse has it.

explanations.answer: He has gone to Judah instead
explanations.explanation: Judah isn't a hiding place in this verse. Hosea 5:5 even says Judah stumbles right along with Israel and Ephraim. The text only says, “He has withdrawn Himself from them.” It doesn't say where He went.
Yes, and it's both. The verse says, “Now the New Moon will devour them along with their land.” Not just the people, the land too. That's a lot to take in, so I'll just say it plainly.
Look at the end of the verse. It says, “Now the New Moon will devour them along with their land.” So the land is in it too. The LORD names both the people and the land.
That's it. The verse says, “raise the battle cry in Beth-aven…” The ram's horn goes in Gibeah and the trumpet in Ramah. Horn, trumpet and battle cry make a loud list.
Nobody's singing a victory song here. The verse says, “raise the battle cry in Beth-aven…” A battle cry is what the text calls for, and a victory song isn't in the verse.

A cry for mercy is a different sound than this verse calls for. The text says, “raise the battle cry in Beth-aven…” The ram's horn and the trumpet already set the mood. They don't sound like a quiet moment.
True, baker. The verse says, “Ephraim will be laid waste on the day of rebuke.” Then the LORD adds, “Among the tribes of Israel I proclaim what is certain.” He doesn't say maybe.
The verse says the opposite. It says, “Ephraim will be laid waste on the day of rebuke.” The LORD also says, “Among the tribes of Israel I proclaim what is certain.” He doesn't say maybe.

Water, right. The LORD says, “I will pour out My fury upon them like water.” Water pours and spreads out and doesn't stop at the edge of the table. That's a lot of fury, and I'll leave it right there.
Oil does pour, I'll give you that. But the verse says, “I will pour out My fury upon them like water.” So the answer is water. Oil belongs in another passage.

Sand does pour, but slowly, and the verse doesn't use it. The LORD says, “I will pour out My fury upon them like water.” That's the word for the blank. Any baker who's spilled flour knows how far a spill spreads, and water spreads even farther.

explanations.answer: He is determined to follow worthless idols
explanations.explanation: Yes. The verse says Ephraim is “…oppressed, crushed in judgment, for he is determined to follow worthless idols.” The text gives the reason right there. Determined is a strong word, too.

explanations.answer: He refused to pay tribute to Judah
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions tribute to Judah. It says Ephraim is crushed in judgment “…for he is determined to follow worthless idols.” That's the reason the verse gives, and I won't swap in one it doesn't.

explanations.answer: He stopped bringing offerings to the LORD
explanations.explanation: That doesn't match the text. In Hosea 5:6 they go with their flocks and herds to seek the LORD. The reason for the judgment in verse 11 is that “…he is determined to follow worthless idols.”
Decay, that's right. The LORD says, “So I am like a moth to Ephraim, and like decay to the house of Judah.” A moth and decay aren't a thunderclap. They're the slow kind of trouble.
Thunder is loud, and this picture is the quiet kind. The LORD says He is like a moth to Ephraim and “…like decay to the house of Judah.” The word that fits the blank is decay.
Hail would be a big dramatic picture, but it isn't the one in the verse. The LORD says, “…like decay to the house of Judah.” So the blank is decay. Moth and decay are small things.
Yes. The verse says, “…then Ephraim turned to Assyria and sent to the great king.” Assyria is the nation Ephraim looks to for help. The LORD then says that king “…cannot cure you or heal your wound.”

Egypt, huh? Famous name, big résumé, but it didn't make it into this verse. Hosea 5:13 says, “…then Ephraim turned to Assyria and sent to the great king.” Assyria is the answer, and Egypt can go sit back down.

Babylon isn't named in this verse. The text says, “…then Ephraim turned to Assyria and sent to the great king.” Assyria is where Ephraim sends for help. I'd rather give the right address than guess one.
I wish that were so, but the LORD says otherwise. The verse says, “But he cannot cure you or heal your wound.” The great king can't do either one. Ephraim sent to the wrong place for a cure.
Right. Ephraim sends to the great king, but the LORD says, “But he cannot cure you or heal your wound.” The king can't do either one. Ephraim sent to the wrong place for a cure.

explanations.answer: Go away and carry them off
explanations.explanation: Yes. The LORD says, “I, even I, will tear them to pieces and then go away. I will carry them off where no one can rescue them.” That's a heavy verse, and I think it's okay to feel that. I'll just let the verse say it.

explanations.answer: Stay and stand guard over them
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of the verse. The LORD says He will tear them to pieces “…and then go away.” He doesn't say He stays. This is one of the harder verses in the passage.

explanations.answer: Return them to their own land
explanations.explanation: The verse says something different. The LORD says, “I will carry them off where no one can rescue them.” Nothing there about sending them home. Returning is a bigger idea in other places, but it isn't in this verse.
I understand wanting a rescue, but the verse closes that door. The LORD says He will carry them off “…where no one can rescue them.” No one means no one. It's a hard line.
That's right. The LORD says, “I will carry them off where no one can rescue them.” So nobody is going to step in and rescue Ephraim and Judah. It's a heavy ending to the lion picture.
Guilt is right. The LORD says He will return to His place “…until they admit their guilt and seek My face…” Admitting guilt is hard. I've had to say a few things out loud myself.
Face, baker. The LORD says they will “…seek My face…” He doesn't say seek My gifts or My help, He says seek My face. Faces are for looking at the one you want to see.
Wealth isn't what the LORD asks for here. The verse says they will admit their guilt and seek His face. Wealth doesn't fit either blank. Not a single coin in this verse.
A crown would be fancy, but the verse doesn't mention one. The LORD says, “…until they admit their guilt and seek My face…” So the blanks are guilt and face. Crowns can stay on the shelf.

Gifts aren't in this verse. The LORD says He will stay in His place “…until they admit their guilt and seek My face…” Hosea 5:6 already told us the people brought flocks and herds and still didn't find Him. So the blank is about what they admit and who they seek.

explanations.answer: Heal us and bind up our wounds
explanations.explanation: That's the turn. The call says, “For He has torn us to pieces, but He will heal us; He has wounded us, but He will bind up our wounds.” The word “but” is doing a lot of work in that sentence. I like where that word takes us.

explanations.answer: Give us a new king to follow
explanations.explanation: The call doesn't ask for a new king. It says, “He has wounded us, but He will bind up our wounds.” It's about healing, not about who sits on a throne.

explanations.answer: Choose a new people for Himself
explanations.explanation: The call goes in another direction. It says, “For He has torn us to pieces, but He will heal us…” The people are still the people, and He's the one who heals them. Nothing about replacing anybody.
True, baker. The call says, “After two days He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up…” Revive first, then raise up. It's a two-step, and both steps are His.
The call says the opposite. It says, “After two days He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up…” So the third day is right there in the verse. Two days, then the third.

explanations.answer: That we may live in His presence
explanations.explanation: Yes. The call says, “on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live in His presence.” The point is to be with Him. That's about the best reason I can think of.

explanations.answer: That we may defeat our enemies
explanations.explanation: I get the thought, but the verse doesn't say that. It says He will raise us up “…that we may live in His presence.” So the reason is living in His presence, and nothing about enemies.

explanations.answer: That we may rebuild our cities
explanations.explanation: Rebuilding cities sounds like honest work, but it isn't what the call says. The verse says He will raise us up “…that we may live in His presence.” That's the reason it gives. No bricks, no blueprints, just His presence.
Right. The call says, “As surely as the sun rises, He will appear…” The sun rising is the picture of something you can count on. So His appearing is just as sure.

explanations.answer: It will only happen in the morning
explanations.explanation: The sun comparison isn't about the time of day. The call says, “As surely as the sun rises, He will appear…” The sun is the picture of something certain. It doesn't set a clock for when He appears.

explanations.answer: It will happen just one time
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say how many times. It says, “As surely as the sun rises, He will appear…” So I won't put a number on it. What the verse tells us is that it's certain.

Rain, that's it. The call says, “He will come to us like the rain, like the spring showers that water the earth.” Rain is something the earth is glad to see. It's a gentle ending after a rough passage.
Wind is a fair guess, but the call says rain. The verse says, “He will come to us like the rain, like the spring showers that water the earth.” Spring showers water the earth, so that's the picture.
Fire is in the oven for me, friend, and it isn't in this verse. The call says, “He will come to us like the rain, like the spring showers that water the earth.” So the answer is rain.
